coredata.dc:description: Dimethylbisphenol A (DMBPA) is a novel alternative to bisphenol A. Whether short-term exposure to DMBPA affects Leydig cell regeneration remains unknown. The Leydig cell regeneration model was generated by intraperitoneal injection of 75 mg/kg ethane dimethane sulfonate (EDS) to adult male Sprague-Dawley rats. Leydig cell regeneration began on day 14 after EDS. Rats were gavaged with 0, 10, 50, or 200 mg/kg DMBPA from days 14–28 post-EDS, and Leydig cell regeneration was assessed on days 28 and 56 post-EDS. DMBPA significantly reduced serum testosterone levels on days 28 and 56 at 10 mg/kg and higher doses and sperm count in the caudal epididymis on day 56 at 200 mg/kg, without affecting estradiol, luteinizing hormone, and follicle-stimulating hormone. DMBPA had no effect on Leydig cell number but significantly down-regulated Scarb1 expression at ≥ 10 mg/kg on day 28, Cyp17a1 expression on day 28 at 200 mg/kg and on day 56 at ≥ 10 mg/kg. DMBPA markedly upregulated Srd5a1 expression at doses of 50 and 200 mg/kg on day 56 after EDS. DMBPA significantly down-regulated the expression of Sod1 and Nr3c4 at a dose of 200 mg/kg on day 28. Further semi-quantitative immunohistochemistry showed that DMBPA reduced NR3C4 levels in Leydig and Sertoli cells at 50 and 200 mg/kg. In vitro DMBPA treatment of immature Leydig cells for 24 h showed that it significantly reduced testosterone production at 10 and 50 μM, and further mechanistic studies showed that an NR3C4 agonist 7α-methyl-19-nortestosterone significantly reversed DMBPA-mediated suppression on testosterone output, but the estrogen receptor antagonist ICI 182,780 and G-coupled estrogen receptor 1 agonist G15 had no effect. In conclusion, DMBPA delays Leydig cell regeneration after short-term exposure during early Leydig cell regeneration via NR3C4 antagonism.

ce:section.ce:para: Many environmental pollutants including bisphenols (Li et al., 2020) and triphenyl phosphate (Ma et al., 2021) are endocrine disrupting chemicals, which not only interfere with estrogen and androgen receptors but also disrupting normal steroidogenesis. Bisphenol A (BPA) is widely used in the formulation of epoxy resins, phenolic resins, and polycarbonate plastics. BPA has been used to manufacture a variety of everyday household items such as plastic baby bottles, thermal paper products, food containers, and kitchen utensils. Numerous studies have reported its endocrine-disrupting effects, including effects on the male reproductive endocrine system, because BPA weakly binds estrogen receptor α (ESR1) (Kitamura et al., 2005) and G-coupled estrogen receptor 1 (GPER1) as an agonist when compared to natural ligand 17β-estradiol (E2)(Cimmino et al., 2019) and binds androgen receptor (NR3C4) as an antagonist (Kitamura et al., 2005). Its endocrine-disrupting effect has drawn great attention and its application is restricted by regulatory agencies worldwide [see review (Li et al., 2020)]. To this end, many BPA analogs, including 3,3'-dimethylbisphenol A (DMBPA, also called bisphenol C, BPC), have been introduced to the market as alternatives. DMBPA has been reported as alternative of BPA in thermal paper (EPA, 2015). Although the use of DMBPA is just beginning, the presence of DMBPA has been detected in bottled beverages (Mandrah et al., 2017) and wastewater (Cesen et al., 2018), indicating that it can be exposed to humans. However, the toxicity of DMBPA is largely lacking.

A reporter luciferase screening assay for BPA analogs in the human breast cancer MCF-7 cell line showed that DMBPA also had an estrogenic activity with approximately 2-fold greater potency than BPA to bind human ESR1, and the assay in the mouse fibroblast cell line NIH3T3 showed that DMBPA had androgen antagonistic activity with approximately 7-fold greater potency than BPA to bind mouse NR3C4 (Kitamura et al., 2005). This indicates that DMBPA may have endocrine-disrupting effects like BPA.

Adult Leydig cells are a major source of androgens (mainly testosterone, T), which play a key role in maintaining male secondary sexual characteristics, stimulating spermatogenesis, and increasing muscle and bone strength (Li et al., 2022). Adult Leydig cells also secrete insulin-like 3 (INSL3), a good biomarker for mature Leydig cells (Li et al., 2022). Pituitary gonadotrophs secrete luteinizing hormone (LH), which reaches LH receptors (LHCGR) on the surface of Leydig cells to stimulate T biosynthesis. T synthesis starts from the substrate cholesterol, is taken up by the high-density lipoprotein receptor (SCARB1) and enters cell cytoplasm, and is further transported by the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (STAR) to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme (CYP11A1) catalyzes it to pregnenolone. Pregnenolone diffuses into the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, where 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (HSD3B1), 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase (CYP17A1) and 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 3 (HSD17B3) catalyze sequential reactions from pregnenolone to T (Li et al., 2022).

Adult Leydig cells originate from stem Leydig cells, which undergo a series of transitions from stem cells to progenitor Leydig cells with the appearance of biomarkers of 5α-reductase 1 (SRD5A1) and 3α-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (AKR1C14), to immature Leydig cells with the appearance of biomarker of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 1 (HSD11B1), and finally to adult Leydig cells (Li et al., 2022). This process can occur not only in pubertal testes, but also in adult testes in which Leydig cells are eliminated by ethane dimethane sulfonate (EDS) treatment (Li et al., 2022; Stanley et al., 2012).

The development and regeneration of Leydig cells depends not only on the intrinsic transcription factor steroidogenic factor-1 (NR5A1), but also on the regulation of LH, steroid hormones including T and estrogen E2, and growth factors secreted by Sertoli cells such as dessert hedgehog (DHH) and anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), which are regulated by follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) through its receptor (FSHR) and transcription factor (SOX9) (Li et al., 2022). Androgens bind to its receptor NR3C4 to exert effects. NR3C4 exists in stem Leydig cells (Kilcoyne et al., 2014) and reaches expression peak in immature Leydig cells during the developmental process (Shan et al., 1995). Conditional knockout of NR3C4 in the Leydig cell lineage can significantly delay Leydig cell maturation (O'Hara et al., 2014), while supplementing androgen can significantly stimulate the maturation of progenitor and immature Leydig cells (Hardy et al., 1990; Li et al., 2021; Sencar et al., 2021), indicating that androgens play an autocrine regulatory role in Leydig cell development. NR3C4 is also present in Sertoli cells and peritubular myoid cells. Conditional knockout of NR3C4 in Sertoli cells and peritubular myoid cells also blocked Leydig cell differentiation, suggesting that androgens exert paracrine regulation of Leydig cell development through NR3C4 in other testicular cells (Chang et al., 2004; Welsh et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2007). In the contrast, estrogen plays a negative regulation on Leydig cell development because ESR1 and GPER1 exist in the Leydig cell lineage and knockout of ESR1 can cause Leydig cell hyperplasia and increased T levels in mice (Akingbemi, 2005), and supplementing GPER1 agonist G1 to Leydig cells can inhibit Leydig cell steroidogenesis (Vaucher et al., 2014).

EDS-induced Leydig cell elimination and then regeneration from stem Leydig cells in the adult testis is an excellent model to investigate the effects of chemicals on Leydig cell regeneration (Stanley et al., 2012). In this model, a single intraperitoneal injection of EDS significantly eliminates Leydig cells within 4 days, and then from day 14 post EDS, Leydig cells regenerate from stem cells to progenitor cells and immature cells (day 28 post EDS) and eventually mature into adult Leydig cells on day 56 after EDS (Guo et al., 2013). The effects of DMBPA on the developmental/regeneration process of adult Leydig cell population and its underlying mechanism remain unclear. In this study, we examined the regeneration of Leydig cells by gavage of DMBPA from days 14–28 after EDS and observed changes in serum hormones and Leydig cell function.

DMBPA (CAS no. 79–97–0, purity >98.0 % analyzed by GC) was obtained from Tokyo Chemical Industry Co., Ltd. (Tokyo, Japan). Sixty-four 49-day-old male Sprague-Dawley rats were purchased from Shanghai Jihui Experimental Animal Breeding Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). The animal study was approved by the Animal Care and Use Ethics Committee of Wenzhou Medical University, and was conducted in accordance with the Guidelines for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Supplementary Table S1 showed qPCR primer names, gene names, forward and reverse primer sequences, PCR product size, and gene accession number. The primers were synthesized by Sangon Biotechnology (Shanghai, China). Supplementary Table S2 showed the primary and secondary antibodies used for immunohistochemistry and Western blot.

Rats were housed under the following conditions: 12 h dark: 12 h light cycle, temperature 21–25 °C, relative humidity 45–55%. Rats were fed with regular chow (total energy content 167 KJ/100 g) from Shanghai Laboratory Animal Center. After 7 days of adjustment, each rat was intraperitoneally injected with 75 mg/kg body weight of EDS to kill adult Leydig cells as previously described (Guo et al., 2013). Then, rats were randomly divided into 4 groups (16 animals per group, 8 rats per time point per group on days 28 and 56 after EDS, respectively): 0, 10, 50, and 200 mg/kg DMBPA. Rats were gavaged from days 14–28 after EDS, covering the earlier developmental period from stem Leydig cells into immature Leydig cells (Stanley et al., 2012). The vehicle used to deliver DMBPA was corn oil (Sigma; CAS no. 8001–30–7) at 2 ml/kg body weight. Doses were selected based on previous bisphenol AF (a BPA analog) toxicity study, in which the DMBPA analog bisphenol AF significantly reduced T levels on day 28 after EDS at 10–200 mg/kg (Yu et al., 2022). Toxicological parameters including body weight, testicular weight and, epididymal weight were recorded for each rat on days 28 and 56 after EDS. Rats were euthanized by CO2 followed by cervical dislocation. A tube of trunk blood was collected immediately for serum separation. Serum samples were stored at − 20 °C for T, E2, LH, and FSH measurement. One testis per rat was frozen at − 80 °C for mRNA and protein studies. Contralateral testes were fixed in Bouin's solution for immunohistochemistry.

Total T levels in serum samples were measured using an Immulite 2000 T chemiluminescent immunoassay kit as described previously (Wu et al., 2017). The limit of detection of T was 0.2 ng/ml and the cross-reactivity of the kit was 2%, 0.6%, 0.5%, and 0.1% for 5α-dihydrotestosterone, androstenedione, 5α-androstane-3β, 17-diol, and progesterone, respectively. Inter-assay co-variances were within 15%.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Determination of serum E2, LH, and FSH levels
ce:section.ce:para: Serum levels of E2, LH, and FSH were determined by ELISA using rat E2, LH, FSH ELISA kits (Shanghai Jianglai Industrial Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, linear regression was made with different concentrations of standards. Serum samples were combined with peroxidase-labeled IgG anti-E2, anti-LH or anti-FSH antibody attached to the wells of a 96-well plate, followed by enzymatic reaction and substrate supplement and measured at 450 nm with a microplate reader. Finally, the concentration in each sample was calculated according to the linear equation. The limit of detection of E2 was 0.1 pmol/l and the limits of detection of LH and FSH concentrations were 0.1 mIU/ml.

Testes were processed, embedded in paraffin, and 1.5 mm2 block of each sample was assembled in a tissue-array tray, and 5 µm sections were cut. HSD11B1 was used as a biomarker for labeling immature and mature Leydig cells (Guo et al., 2013). CYP11A1 was used as a biomarker for all Leydig cells (Guo et al., 2013), SOX9 was used as a biomarker for Sertoli cells (Koopman, 1999). Briefly, tissue sections were de-paraffinized and rehydrated following standard procedures. Endogenous peroxidase activity was quenched by immersing the slices in 3% (v/v) hydrogen peroxide in Tris-buffered saline for 10 min at room temperature. Then, heat-induced antigen retrieval was performed by boiling the tissue sections in 0.01 M citrate buffer (pH 6.0) for 3 min. Sections were incubated in 10% goat serum for 30 min to block antibody binding to non-specific epitopes. Sections were incubated with a series of primary antibodies (HSD11B1, CYP11A1, SOX9, and NR3C4, each in 1:200 dilution) at 4 °C and then secondary antibody was incubated for 30 min at room temperature The localization of the primary antibody was visualized by adding the chromogenic peroxidase substrate 3, 3'-diaminobenzidine (DAB). Sections were counterstained with hematoxylin, dehydrated, and mounted on glass coverslips. The slides were scanned to the digital files by NanoZoomer-XR (Hamamatsu, Japan) at 0.23 µm per pixel. Since rat Sertoli cells did not change after 21 days of age (Hutchison et al., 2008), we adjusted Leydig cell number to Sertoli cells.

The scanned image was displayed by Image-Pro Plus software (version 6, Media Cybernetics, Inc. Rockville, MD). NR3C4 staining in Leydig cells, Sertoli cells, and peritubular myoid cells and the nearby background staining were selected using Selection Tool of the software. The mean density was calculated and exported to a Microsoft Excel worksheet and the net density was calculated by subtracting the background density from NR3C4 density.

ce:section.ce:section-title: RNA isolation, reverse transcription, and qPCR
ce:section.ce:para: RNA isolation, reverse transcription, and qPCR were performed as previously described (Guo et al., 2013). Briefly, RNA in testis and pituitary was purified using the Trizol kit. The aqueous layer was separated from the organic layer by chloroform and isopropanol was added to the aqueous layer to extract total RNA. RNA was dissolved in RNase-free water and RNA concentration was read for O.D at 260 nm by NanoDrop 2000. A reverse transcription kit (Vazyme, Nanjing, China) was performed to reverse transcribe RNA to cDNA. The cDNA was amplified using SYBR Green qPCR Kit in CFX96 Touch Deep Well system (Bio-Rad, USA). Expression of the following genes was measured: Lhcgr encoding LHCGR for LH signaling, Scarb1 encoding the high-density lipoprotein receptor (SCARB1) for cholesterol uptake, Star encoding steroidogenic acute regulatory protein (STAR) for cholesterol transport regulation, Cyp11a1, Hsd3b1, Cyp17a1, Hsd17b3, Srd5a1, and Hsd11b1 encoding the corresponding steroidogenic enzymes CYP11A1, HSD3B1, CYP17A1, HSD17B3, SRD5A1 and HSD11B1, and Nr5a1 encoding a nuclear transcription factor (NR5A1), Fshr encoding FSH receptor (FSHR) for FSH signaling in Sertoli cells, Dhh encoding desert hedgehog (DHH) secreted by Sertoli cells to regulate Leydig cell development, and Sox9 encoding SOX9. The expression of antioxidant genes (Sod1, Sod2, Cat, and Gpx1), apoptosis-related genes (Bcl2 and Bax), Esr1, Gper, and Nr3c4 were also determined in the testis. Ct values were recorded and mRNA levels were calculated using the linear equation of the Ct value versus the logarithm of the diluted standard. Actb and Rps16 are housekeeping genes. Since there were no changes between the control and DMBPA groups for Actb and Rps16, their mRNA levels were finally normalized to Actb mRNA.

Testes collected on days 28 and 56 after EDS were used. Protein sample preparation and Western blot were performed as previously described (Yu et al., 2022). Briefly, testes were homogenized and protein concentrations were measured using a BCA kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China). Total protein (30 μg) was loaded and electrophoresed on a 10% polyacrylamide gel, and the separated proteins were transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane. Membranes were blocked with 5% non-fat milk in TBST buffer for 2 h, followed by primary antibodies against SCARB1 (1:1000, v/v), CYP17A1 (1:1000), SRD5A1 (1:1000), SOD1 (1:1000), NR3C4 (1:1000), SIRT1 (1:1000), PGC1α (1:2000), ERK1/2 (1:1000), pERK1/2 (1:5000), and ACTB (1:1000) at 4 °C overnight. Membranes were subsequently washed and incubated with HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit (1:2000) or anti-mouse (1:2000) for 2 h at room temperature, and protein bands were ECL visualized using an ECL kit (Thomas Scientific, USA). The target protein was adjusted to the internal control ACTB. Protein intensities were measured using Image Lab software (Bio-Rad).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Leydig cell isolation and primary cell culture
ce:section.ce:para: Leydig cells on day 28 after EDS belong to immature Leydig cells, which have the highest expression of NR3C4 (Shan and Hardy, 1992). Immature Leydig cells were isolated from rat testis on day 28 after EDS as previously described (Guo et al., 2013). Briefly, a total of three rats were used each time for cell isolation and four independent isolations were done. Rats were euthanized under CO2. Testes were removed and digested with collagenase D (0.25 mg/ml) and DNase (0.25 mg/ml) for 15 min at 34 °C. Subsequently, the cell supernatant was filtered through a 100 µm nylon mesh and was subjected to continuous Percoll gradient centrifugation. Immature Leydig cells were collected at a specific density of 1.070–1.088 g/ml and the purity was determined by HSD3B1 enzymatic method as previously described (Payne et al., 1980) and typically 95% purity of Leydig cells was achieved. Cells were immediately seeded into the 12-well culture plate at a density of 5 × 105 cells/well in 1 ml of DMEM: F12 (1: 1, vol/vol) containing 0, 0.1, 1, 10, and 50 μM DMBPA, 100 nM ICI 182,780 (ICI), 100 nM G15, 100 nM MENT or various concentrations with DMBPA in combination with 100 nM ICI, or 100 nM G15, and 100 nM MENT for 24 h. ICI (Akingbemi et al., 2003) is a specific ESR1 antagonist and G15 (Cimmino et al., 2019) is a specific GPER1 antagonist. MENT is a synthetic potent NR3C4 agonist (Li et al., 2021). After the treatment of DMBPA, Leydig cells were stained by HSD3B1 enzymatic staining agent for morphological changes and HSD3B1 activity.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Ultra high performance-MS/MS determination of medium T concentration
ce:section.ce:para: T in medium was determined with an Acquity ultra-high performance liquid chromatography unit and a XEVO TQD triple quadrupole mass spectrometer (Waters Corp., USA) as previously described (Zhao et al., 2021). Briefly, the T-d5 internal solution (10 μl) was added to 100 μl culture medium collected, and then mixed with 200 μl acetonitrile, and centrifuged at 12,000g for 15 min. The T working solution was diluted from the stock solution with methanol and calibration standards and quality control samples with T-free medium and extracted with acetonitrile in parallel. The supernatant (1 μl) of each sample was injected into the HPLC-MS/MS system through an auto-sampler. The intra-assay and inter-assay coefficient of variation was less than 15%.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Ultra high performance-MS/MS determination of serum DMBPA concentration
ce:section.ce:para: DMBPA in the serum was measured with a Waters Xevo TQ-S triple quadrupole tandem mass spectrometer (Milford, MA) connecting with a Waters ACQUITY UPLC I-Class system (Milford, MA). Before analysis, we optimized and confirmed the mass spectrometric parameters as previously described (Zhang et al., 2022). We implemented the measurement in negative ion mode using multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) with an electrospray ionization source (ESI). We manipulated data using the Quanlynx program with Masslynx 4.1 software (Milford, MA). The internal substance (IS) was furosemide, which was added to the serum samples for normalization.

After incubation at 37 °C for 15 min, 0.5 ml of sperm suspension was transferred from the petri dish to 2 ml PBS, and incubated at 60 °C for 1 min. Data are presented as mean ± SEM. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Differences between two groups were conducted by one-way ANOVA followed by post hoc Dunnett's multiple comparisons to compare with the control. For Western blotting data, the paired Student “t” test was used, and Sidak adjustment was recalculated for the p value. GraphPad Prism 8.0.1 (La Jolla, CA) was used.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of DMBPA on body weight, testicular, and epididymal weight
ce:section.ce:para: Compared to BPA ( Fig. 1A), DMBPA (Fig. 1B) has one methyl group at the 3-position of each phenyl ring. DMBPA was dosed from days 14–28 post EDS and the Leydig cell regeneration was observed on days 28 and 56 after EDS. No overt toxicity was observed during the course of DMBPA exposure. The body weight, testicular weight, and epididymal weight were not significantly altered on days 28 and 56 after EDS ( Table 1).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Serum hormone levels and sperm amount in the epididymis
ce:section.ce:para: Serum T levels were significantly reduced by ≥ 10 mg/kg DMBPA on days 28 and 56 post EDS (Fig. 1D), indicating that LC regeneration is delayed by DMBPA. Serum E2 levels were not altered after DMBPA exposure (Fig. 1E). Serum levels of LH and FSH on both time-points were also not altered after DMBPA exposure (Figs. 1F and 1G). DMBPA significantly reduced that sperm amount in the epididymal cauda at 200 mg/kg (Fig. 1H).

Compared to day 28 after EDS, both CYP11A1+ (Fig.S1) and HSD11B1+ (Fig.S2) Leydig cell number was almost doubled, confirming that there is a round of mitosis of Leydig cells from days 28–56 post EDS. However, DMBPA exposure did not alter the Leydig cell number, indicating that DMBPA does not affect Leydig cell proliferation and apoptosis.

The expression levels of Leydig cell genes (Lhcgr, Scarb1, Star, Cyp11a1, Hsd3b1, Cyp17a1, Hsd17b3, Insl3, and Nr5a1) and Sertoli cell genes (Sox9, Amh, and Dhh) were measured by qPCR. DMBPA significantly down-regulated Scarb1 expression on day 28 after EDS at ≥ 10 mg/kg, and this repression was recovered on day 56 post EDS. DMBPA markedly down-regulated Cyp17a1 expression on day 28 after EDS at 200 mg/kg, and its suppression gained more severe on day 56 post EDS, with the marked inhibition being seen as low as 10 mg/kg. However, the expression of Srd5a1, a biomarker of immature Leydig cells (Guo et al., 2013), was significantly up-regulated by DMBPA at 50 and 200 mg/kg on day 56 post EDS ( Fig. 2). These data indicate that DMBPA delays Leydig cell maturation. However, DMBPA did not affect the expression of Amh, Dhh, and Sox9.

The levels of Leydig cell proteins (SCARB1 and CYP17A1) on day 28 after EDS and CYP17A1 and SRD5A1 on day 56 after EDS were determined by Western blot. SCARB1 was significantly reduced at 50 and 200 mg/kg on day 28 post EDS, CYP17A1 was significantly reduced at 10 mg/kg and higher doses on days 28 and 56 after EDS, while SRD5A1 was significantly increased on day 56 after EDS at 50 and 200 mg/kg ( Fig. 3). This result largely conformed to their mRNA changes.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Expression of estrogen and androgen receptors
ce:section.ce:para: To explore the underlying mechanism of DMBPA, we measured the expression of genes and proteins associated with estrogen and androgen receptors, as previous studies have shown that BPA and DMBPA can bind ESR1 and GPER1 as agonists and NR3C4 as an antagonist (Li et al., 2020). QPCR showed that the expression of Nr3c4 was significantly down-regulated by 200 mg/kg DMBPA on day 28 after EDS, but not on day 56, while the expression of Esr1 and Gper was unaltered ( Fig. 4A). Further Western blot revealed that NR3C4 levels were significantly reduced by 50 and 200 mg/kg DMBPA on day 28 after EDS (Fig. 4B). Previous studies have shown that NR3C4 was expressed in Leydig cells, Sertoli cells, and peritubular myoid cells and all expression was critical for Leydig cell development (Denolet et al., 2006; Hazra et al. 2014; O'Hara et al., 2014; Welsh et al., 2009). We measured NR3C4 density in Leydig cells, Sertoli cells, and peritubular myoid cells using a semi-quantitative immunohistochemistry. Indeed, NR3C4 was expressed in all three testicular cell types. DMBPA significantly reduced NR3C4 density in Leydig cells and Sertoli cells without changing its density in peritubular myoid cells at 50 and 200 mg/kg (Fig. 4C-G), indicating that DMBPA mainly targets NR3C4 in Leydig cells and Sertoli cells.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Expression of antioxidants and MDA levels
ce:section.ce:para: Previous studies have also shown that BPA and BPA analogs can induce oxidative stress and possibly apoptosis (Meng et al., 2019; Rahman et al., 2019). We measured the expression of genes and proteins related to antioxidants and apoptosis. The QPCR data showed that only the expression of Sod1 was slightly but significantly decreased in the 200 mg/kg DMBPA group on day 28 post EDS, whereas the expression of Sod2, Gpx1, Cat, Bax, and Bcl2 was not altered by DMBPA on days 28 and 56 ( Fig. 5A). We further performed Western blot to detect SOD1 levels on day 28 after EDS and found that DMBPA significantly reduced SOD1 levels at 200 mg/kg on day 28 after EDS (Fig. 5B and C). We also measured testicular MDA levels on day 28 after EDS and found no changes (Fig. 5D). This suggests that DMBPA did not induce significant oxidative stress despite SOD1 reduction.

Several signaling pathways, including SIRT1/PGC1α and ERK1/2 signaling pathways, are involved in Leydig cell maturation (Chung et al., 2021; Gak et al., 2015; Matzkin et al., 2013). We measured levels of SIRT1, PGC1α and total ERK1/2 as well as phosphorylated ERK1/2 and found that DMBPA significantly reduced SIRT1 and PGC1α at 50 and 200 mg/kg and reduced phosphorylation of ERK1/2 at 200 mg/kg ( Fig. 6).

ce:section.ce:section-title: The effect of DMBPA on T synthesis in primary Leydig cells
ce:section.ce:para: To explore whether DMBPA had a direct effect on Leydig cell steroidogenesis and its underlying mechanisms, we used the specific ESR1 antagonist ICI, the specific GPER1 antagonist G15, and the specific NR3C4 agonist MENT alone or in combination with DMBPA, because immature Leydig cells have the highest expression of NR3C4, ESR1 and GPER1. ICI and G15 alone significantly increased T output, confirming that endogenous estrogen secreted by immature stromal cells negatively affects T biosynthesis. MENT also markedly increased T output, further confirming that androgens are required for T biosynthesis in immature Leydig cells. After treatment with different concentrations of DMBPA, Leydig cell morphology and HSD3B1 staining were not changed (Fig. S3), while T output was significantly decreased at 10 and 50 μM with IC50 values of 3.76 μM, and the combination of ICI or G15 with DMBPA did not reverse DMBPA-mediated inhibition of T output with IC50 values of between 2.49 and 3.13 μM. However, MENT completely reversed DMBPA-mediated inhibition of T output. This suggests that DMBPA can bind NR3C4 to inhibit T biosynthesis from immature Leydig cells ( Fig. 7).

ce:section.ce:section-title: The determination of serum DMBPA levels
ce:section.ce:para: The representative MRM chromatogram peaks of DMBPA in the methanol and rat blank plasma sample spiked with IS (furosemide), and rat plasma sample after 200 mg/kg DMBPA treatment spiked with IS (furosemide) showed that the plasma interfered with the detection peak of DMBPA but not IS (Supplementary Fig. S4), indicating that DMBPA may bind to some proteins in the plasma or the serum interferes with the DMBPA detection.

In this study, we demonstrate that exposure to DMBPA during the commitment of stem Leydig cells to the Leydig cell lineage significantly delays later regeneration. This inhibition is due to down-regulation of some key steroidogenesis-related genes (Scarb1 and Cyp17a1). Apparently, down-regulation of NR3C4 in Leydig and Sertoli cells is associated with this delay.

Exposure to DMBPA on days 14–28 post EDS resulted in delayed Leydig cell regeneration on days 28 and 56 post EDS, as evidenced by the following results: 1) Serum T levels on days 28 and 56 post-EDS were significantly reduced at 10 mg/kg and higher doses (Fig. 1D); 2) the expression of Leydig cell genes Scarb1 and Cyp17a1 and their proteins [mature biomarkers (Guo et al., 2013)] was significantly down-regulated on day 28 after EDS, and Cyp17a1 was significantly down-regulated on day 56 after EDS; 3) the expression of the Leydig cell gene Srd5a1 and its protein [immature Leydig cell biomarker (Guo et al., 2013)] was significantly up-regulated on day 56 after EDS. Apparently, the decrease in serum T was not due to changes in the number of Leydig cells and serum LH and FSH levels, as the number of Leydig cells and serum LH and FSH levels did not change after DMBPA exposure.

In the previous study (Yu et al., 2022), we also performed the effects of BPA analog BPAF on Leydig cell regeneration after EDS treated with 0, 10, 100, and 200 mg/kg BPAF from days 7–28 post EDS and found that BPAF significantly reduced serum T levels at ≥ 10 mg/kg and E2 at 100 and 200 mg/kg, serum LH and FSH at 100/200 mg/kg, significantly reduced CYP11A1+ Leydig cell number and HSD11B1+ Leydig cell number, and down-regulated the expression of Insl3, Star, Cyp17a1, Hsd11b1, Hsd17b3 at various doses. However, in this study, DMBPA did not affect serum E2, LH, and FSH levels, and Leydig cell number, only down-regulated the expression of fewer genes (Scarb1 and Cyp17a1), indicating that DMBPA is less potent than BPAF in the inhibition of Leydig cell regeneration.

Previous studies have shown that BPA and DMBPA can bind to ESR1 as agonists, with DMBPA binding to human ESR1 approximately 2 times more potently than BPA (Kitamura et al., 2005). ESR1 has been shown to negatively regulate T biosynthesis in Leydig cells since knockdown of ESR1 in mice markedly increased T output in Leydig cells (Akingbemi et al., 2003). We found that DMBPA significantly inhibited T secretion from immature Leydig cells in vitro, but its inhibition was not affected by ESR1 antagonism with the specific antagonist ICI, indicating that DMBPA-mediated inhibition is not through ESR1 signaling. GPER1 is also present in rat and human Leydig cells, and it negatively controls T biosynthesis in Leydig cells (Vaucher et al., 2014). While BPA has been shown to bind GPER1 potently, it is unclear whether DMBPA has the ability to bind GPER1 (Chung et al., 2011; Cimmino et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019). However, DMBPA-mediated inhibition of T biosynthesis in immature Leydig cells was not antagonized by the GPER1 antagonist G15 (in this study), suggesting that DMBPA inhibits T biosynthesis not through GPER1.

Previous studies have shown that NR3C4 is essential for the maturation of progenitor and immature Leydig cells into adult Leydig cells (Hardy et al., 1990; Sencar et al., 2021). Potent androgen MENT in vitro can stimulate maturation of Leydig cells by binding to NR3C4, mainly up-regulating Cyp17a1 expression (Sencar et al., 2021). In fact, in Tfm rats and mice, NR3C4 mutation (Le Goascogne et al., 1993; Murphy et al., 1994; Vanderschueren et al., 1993), as well as conditional knockout of NR3C4 in Leydig cells (O'Hara et al., 2014), results in a significant delay in Leydig cell maturation and CYP17A1 was the most sensitive target (Le Goascogne et al., 1993; Murphy et al., 1994; Vanderschueren et al., 1993). In this study, we used MENT, a potent synthetic androgen as NR3C4 agonist, to dissect the underlying mechanism of DMBPA. Indeed, MENT alone can significantly increase androgen output, and it also significantly and completely reversed DMBPA-mediated suppression of T output in primary Leydig cells, suggesting that DMBPA can directly inhibit T biosynthesis through NR3C4 antagonism. In the DMBPA-exposed rats, Cyp17a1 was also the most sensitive to DMBPA and was significantly down-regulated on days 28 and 56 after EDS (Fig. 2).

NR3C4 is also present in Sertoli cells and peritubular myoid cells as a paracrine mechanism, regulating Leydig cells. In fact, conditional knockout of NR3C4 in Sertoli cells prevented Leydig cell maturation (Denolet et al., 2006). We measured the expression of NR3C4 in testicular cells after in vivo exposure and found that DMBPA can significantly reduce the level of NR3C4 in Leydig cells and Sertoli cells. The decrease in NR3C4 may be due to DMBPA antagonism of NR3C4, as androgens positively regulated NR3C4 expression in Sertoli cells and immature Leydig cells of rats (Shan et al., 1997). Down-regulation of NR3C4 in Leydig cells and Sertoli cells further exacerbated the delay in Leydig cell maturation.

Oxidative stress has been found to block Leydig cell steroidogenesis and differentiation and BPA has been found to induce oxidative stress in many cells (El Henafy et al., 2020; Perez-Albaladejo et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2019). Although DMBPA can down-regulate SOD1 expression at the highest dose, it did not induce the increase of MDA, indicating that the oxidative stress after DMBPA exposure is minimal.

In addition to the NR3C4-mediated DMBPA mechanism of suppressing Leydig cell maturation, other signaling pathways may be involved, including SIRT1/PGC1α signaling and ERK1/2 signaling. SIRT1 is an NAD-dependent class III histone deacetylase that deacetylates many targets, such as PGC1α, a transcriptional coactivator that promotes the production of β-oxidative energy from fatty acids (Canto and Auwerx, 2009; Scarpulla, 2011). Down-regulation of SIRT1 and PGC1α was found to be associated with inhibition of steroidogenesis (Chen et al., 2019; Chung et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2012). ERK1/2 is another key responsive protein to certain hormones and growth factors, and indeed, knockdown of the ERK1/2 pathway significantly suppressed Leydig cell steroidogenesis (Matzkin et al., 2013). In this study, we found that DMBPA significantly reduced SIRT1/PGC1α levels and the phosphorylation of ERK1/2, thereby inhibiting Leydig cell regeneration in EDS-treated testes. We cannot detect serum DMBPA levels in the DMBPA-exposed samples, indicating that plasma may interfere with the detection of DMBPA or DMBPA may bind to plasma proteins. So far the DMBPA toxicological data on the endocrine system are largely lacking. No epidemiological study for DMBPA was performed for its effects on endocrine system. The doses used here were selected based on previous studies for BPA (Nakamura et al., 2010) and its analog BPAF (Yu et al., 2022), in which both chemicals at up to 200 mg/kg inhibited serum T levels and down-regulated steroidogenesis-related gene expression. Therefore, exposures in laboratory rats in this study may be higher than in the general population, and we raise some cautions about the extrapolation of our results.

Detectable levels of DMBPA in water systems are of concern due to the increased use of BPA substitutes (Cesen et al., 2018). To the authors' knowledge, DMBPA has been demonstrated for the first time to have endocrine disrupting effects on Leydig cell regeneration. The lack of adequate DMBPA endocrine-disrupting data calls for increased studies in animal models and epidemiology of DMBPA.

This study shows that short-term exposure to DMBPA significantly disrupts Leydig cell regeneration in adult male rats. DMBPA may interfere with Leydig cell regeneration through an NR3C4 antagonistic mechanism. Other signaling pathways such as SIRT1/PGC1α and ERK1/2 may also be involved. Decreased T may cause spermatogenesis to be arrested ( Fig. 8).
